name: Canyon (NYC, 2026)
originator: Founded by Lonti Ebers (former president of MoMA PS1 board, major contemporary art patron). Leadership includes director and curatorial team drawn from time-based media art expertise. Advisory and founding support from major contemporary art figures. [uncertain]
geography: New York City, USA. 40,000 square foot facility. Positioned within the NYC museum ecosystem alongside MoMA, Whitney, New Museum, and others.
core_claim: Time-based media art (video, sound, performance, durational work) deserves dedicated institutional infrastructure at museum scale. Canyon fills a critical gap: no major US museum has been purpose-built for these media. The parallel launch of CMACC (the first US nonprofit conservation center for time-based media) addresses the equally critical archival and preservation gap.
medium_specificity: Entirely medium-specific by design. Canyon is built for art forms that are inherently temporal, immaterial, or process-based -- video, sound, performance, durational work, installation. The architecture is designed for these media rather than adapted from white-cube gallery design. CMACC addresses the specific conservation challenges of time-based media: format obsolescence, equipment dependency, software decay, and the need for migration strategies.
relation_to_attention_economy: Actively resists attention economy logic. Durational and time-based art demands sustained attention from viewers -- the opposite of scroll-based engagement. Canyon's programming model (performance, sound, video that unfolds over time) is structurally anti-attention-economy. The institutional commitment to showing work that requires patience and presence is a deliberate counter to compressed digital attention.
relation_to_intention: Strongly intention-aligned. Canyon serves declared structural needs of the field: dedicated exhibition space for underserved media, conservation infrastructure for at-risk works, institutional legitimacy for time-based practices. This is infrastructure-building driven by identified gaps, not audience capture or engagement optimization. CMACC is pure intention -- conservation infrastructure serves the field's long-term needs regardless of attention.
revenue_model: Nonprofit museum model. Primary revenue from philanthropy (founding donors, grants, endowment), admissions, memberships, and institutional fundraising. CMACC likely operates through grants, institutional partnerships, and service fees for conservation work. No commercial gallery or sales component. Standard US nonprofit arts organization structure. [uncertain]
market_position: Infrastructure and institutional. Canyon is not a market actor but provides institutional legitimacy that supports market value for time-based media artists. CMACC is pure infrastructure -- conservation services that underpin the entire field's sustainability. Positioned as a major institutional addition to the NYC art ecosystem.
price_range: Not applicable as a museum. Canyon does not sell art. However, institutional exhibition and collection validates price levels for represented artists in the broader market.
volume_trend_2024_2026: Opening phase in 2026. Not yet established enough for trend analysis. The opening with a Ryoji Ikeda retrospective signals high ambition and institutional seriousness. Trajectory will depend on programming quality, critical reception, and sustained funding. [uncertain]
collector_demographics: Not directly applicable as a museum. Canyon's audience spans the contemporary art public, with particular appeal to collectors and practitioners of time-based media, sound art, performance, and video art. CMACC serves institutional collectors (museums, foundations) and artists needing conservation services.
sustainability: Dependent on philanthropic infrastructure and endowment sustainability. US nonprofit museum model is well-established but requires ongoing major donor support. The 40,000 sqft facility creates significant operating costs. CMACC may achieve partial self-sustainability through conservation service fees. Long-term sustainability depends on whether Canyon can build an endowment and sustained donor base. The Lonti Ebers connection provides strong initial philanthropic network. [uncertain]
toolchain: Museum-grade AV infrastructure: projection systems, immersive sound design, flexible performance spaces, climate-controlled galleries. CMACC requires specialized conservation equipment: format migration hardware and software, digital preservation systems, media archaeology tools, emulation environments for obsolete formats. Technical infrastructure is purpose-built for time-based media rather than adapted from traditional gallery tech.
relation_to_AI: Not primarily engaged with AI. Canyon's focus on video, sound, performance, and durational art predates and is largely orthogonal to the AI art conversation. However, AI-generated or AI-involved time-based media works could be exhibited. CMACC may need to address AI-specific conservation challenges (preserving works that depend on AI models, dealing with model versioning). The institution is positioned to exhibit AI-engaged work without being defined by it.
liveness: Central to mission. Performance, durational art, and sound installations are inherently live or time-based. Canyon is designed for liveness: real-time performance, evolving installations, sound that unfolds in space and time. This distinguishes it from static-display museums. Even video exhibition involves temporal liveness (works that must be experienced over time). CMACC addresses the paradox of preserving live and ephemeral art forms.
aesthetic_vocabulary: Draws on established vocabulary from video art, sound art, performance studies, and new media art criticism. Terms include: durational, time-based, ephemeral, immersive, site-specific, performative, processual. Canyon's programming will likely contribute to evolving vocabulary around institutional presentation of time-based media. CMACC may develop specialized conservation vocabulary. The critical language is more mature than for generative or blockchain art, built on decades of video art and performance art discourse (Nam June Paik, Bill Viola, Vito Acconci lineage).
tendency_axis_position: Openness <-> Enclosure: Institutional enclosure with public access. Museums are enclosed institutions (curated, gatekept) but serve public access mandates. | Commons <-> Capture: Commons-oriented. Nonprofit conservation center (CMACC) is explicitly commons infrastructure. Museum exhibitions make work publicly accessible. | Spectacle <-> Infrastructure: Both. Exhibition programming has spectacle dimension (Ryoji Ikeda retrospective), but CMACC is pure infrastructure. The balance is intentional. | Individual <-> Collective: Institutional/collective. Canyon serves collective field needs rather than individual market interests.
openness: Partially open. Museum exhibitions are publicly accessible (with admission). CMACC conservation research may produce open-access publications and standards. However, institutional curatorial decisions are enclosed (expert committee/curatorial team). Collection and programming decisions are not community-governed. Standard US museum openness model.
governance_model: Nonprofit board governance with curatorial/directorial leadership. Standard US museum model: board of trustees (major donors, art world figures), executive director, curatorial staff. CMACC likely has advisory board with conservation experts. Decisions made by professional leadership within board-approved strategic framework. Not community-governed or democratic.
data_sovereignty: Institutional control. Canyon owns/controls exhibition documentation, collection records, and institutional data. CMACC conservation records are institutionally held. Artists retain rights over their works per standard museum loan/exhibition agreements. Conservation data sovereignty is a key question: who owns conservation research, migration records, and preservation documentation? Ideally CMACC shares conservation knowledge openly, but institutional incentives may favor enclosure.
interoperability: Moderate. Museum systems use standard cataloging (TMS, similar collection management systems). CMACC could adopt or develop interoperable conservation standards (compatible with efforts like Matters in Media Art, NDSA levels of preservation). No blockchain or API-based interoperability. Institutional interoperability depends on partnerships with other museums and conservation organizations.
preservation_strategy: CMACC is itself a preservation strategy -- the first US nonprofit conservation center dedicated to time-based media. This is Canyon's most significant structural contribution. CMACC likely addresses: format migration (tape to digital, codec preservation), emulation of obsolete playback systems, documentation of performance and installation instructions, creation of preservation best practices for the field. The combination of exhibition space (Canyon) and conservation center (CMACC) creates a vertically integrated preservation infrastructure.
consent_architecture: Standard museum consent frameworks. Artists consent to exhibition through loan agreements. Audiences consent to participation through attendance. CMACC conservation work operates under institutional agreements with artists and lenders. No novel consent architecture specific to digital or time-based media. Machine-readable consent is absent.
relation_to_traditional_art_world: Integration at the highest level. Canyon is a traditional art world institution (major nonprofit museum in NYC, founded by prominent art patron) dedicated to non-traditional media. It represents the traditional art world's institutional embrace of time-based media, not an alternative or parallel system. The Ryoji Ikeda opening retrospective connects to established contemporary art canon.
what_it_enables: Dedicated, purpose-built exhibition space for time-based media art at museum scale in NYC. First US nonprofit conservation center for time-based media (CMACC). Institutional legitimacy for video, sound, performance, and durational art practices. Professional conservation services that could help preserve at-risk works across the field. A model for other cities and institutions to build similar infrastructure.
what_it_lacks: Being a new institution, it lacks established collection depth, curatorial track record, and institutional history. Digital-native art (generative, blockchain, software-based) may not be a primary focus despite the time-based media mandate. Community governance or artist participation in institutional decision-making is likely absent. Global accessibility is limited -- a single NYC location. CMACC's capacity will be limited relative to the enormous scale of at-risk time-based media works globally. [uncertain]
who_is_excluded: Geographically excluded: anyone not in NYC. Economically excluded: museum admission costs (though nonprofits often have free/reduced programs). Artists excluded by curatorial gatekeeping (institutional curation is selective). CMACC services may be inaccessible to independent artists or small organizations without institutional backing. Digital-native artists working in blockchain, generative, or software art may find their practices outside Canyon's primary focus. Communities without institutional connections. [uncertain]
frontier_signal: Emerging institution, established media categories. Canyon itself is frontier as an institution (opening 2026) but the art forms it serves (video, sound, performance) are established. CMACC is more genuinely frontier -- the first US nonprofit conservation center for time-based media fills an identified gap. The institution challenges the category of what a museum should be built for.
discovery_mechanism: Institutional channels: art press, museum marketing, critical reviews, word of mouth within contemporary art world. Opening retrospective (Ryoji Ikeda) generates art press coverage. NYC location provides foot traffic and tourist discovery. Social media presence. Professional networks in conservation (for CMACC). Standard museum discovery model rather than algorithmic or platform-driven.
attention_dependency: Low. Museums generate their own attention through programming, press, and institutional reputation. Canyon does not depend on platform algorithms or social media engagement metrics for survival. Philanthropic funding model is attention-independent. The institution's survival depends on donor relationships and institutional reputation, not attention metrics.
intention_alignment: Strongly intention-native. Canyon addresses declared field needs: dedicated exhibition space for underserved media, conservation infrastructure for at-risk works. CMACC is among the most intention-aligned initiatives in the field -- pure infrastructure serving long-term structural needs. No attention-capture mechanics.
commons_contribution: Significant potential commons contribution. CMACC conservation research, preservation standards, and methodology could be shared openly, benefiting the entire field. Exhibition programming creates public access to time-based media art. If CMACC publishes open-access conservation guidelines, it becomes critical commons infrastructure. The risk is institutional enclosure of conservation knowledge for competitive advantage.
provenance_type: Both ownership and meaning, with emphasis on meaning. Museums create exhibition provenance (institutional context, curatorial framing, critical reception). CMACC creates conservation provenance (preservation history, format migration records, condition documentation). This is richer than ownership-only provenance -- it tracks how works are cared for, contextualized, and preserved over time.
temporal_logic: Archival and durational. Museum temporality is archival (preserving for the future). CMACC operates in deep-historical time (conservation spans decades to centuries). Exhibition programming is cyclical (rotating exhibitions). The focus on durational art creates a unique institutional temporality -- the museum's programming unfolds in time, not just in space.
absence_handling: Directly addresses major field absences. Canyon addresses the absence of dedicated museum space for time-based media in the US. CMACC addresses the absence of nonprofit conservation infrastructure for these media. The institution is explicitly designed to fill identified gaps. However, it may not address the absence of digital-native art infrastructure (generative, blockchain, software) or community-driven alternatives to institutional models.
coherence_vs_consensus: Coherence through curatorial vision. Canyon's programming will reflect curatorial perspectives that create coherence across exhibitions without demanding consensus about what time-based media art is or should be. Multiple valid interpretations and practices can coexist within the institutional framework. CMACC operates closer to consensus -- conservation standards require shared technical agreements.
contestability: Limited. Institutional decisions (programming, acquisitions, conservation priorities) are made by professional leadership and are not formally contestable by the public or artists. Standard museum model: expert authority with public accountability through nonprofit transparency requirements. Artists can decline participation but cannot contest curatorial decisions. CMACC conservation decisions are expert-driven.
forkability: Low for the institution itself (cannot fork a building or endowment). Moderate for CMACC methodologies -- if published openly, conservation approaches can be adopted and adapted by other institutions. The institutional model (purpose-built museum for time-based media) can be replicated in other cities. The physical infrastructure and donor network are not forkable.
what_adai_should_adopt: Canyon's identification of specific structural gaps and building dedicated infrastructure to fill them. CMACC's model of conservation as commons infrastructure. The principle that some field needs require institutional commitment, not just platform innovation. The focus on preservation as a structural concern, not an afterthought. The integration of exhibition (access) and conservation (preservation) in a single institutional framework.
what_adai_should_refuse: The traditional museum governance model (board-donor power dynamics, expert gatekeeping without community input). The geographic concentration in a single elite location (NYC). The potential enclosure of conservation knowledge within institutional boundaries. The absence of digital-native art from the primary mandate. The risk that institutional prestige becomes an end in itself rather than serving field needs.
structural_tension: Canyon represents the traditional art world building infrastructure for non-traditional media. A(DAI) operates outside traditional institutional models. The tension is between institutional stability (Canyon's endowment, building, professional staff) and institutional agility (A(DAI)'s commons-first, digitally native approach). Canyon can preserve works for centuries; A(DAI) aims to build intelligence infrastructure that is alive and evolving. Canyon's CMACC addresses preservation through institutional authority; A(DAI) must address it through distributed, community-owned infrastructure. The question is whether field preservation requires institutional weight or whether new models can achieve comparable permanence.
regulatory_exposure: Standard US nonprofit museum regulations: 501(c)(3) compliance, donor tax deduction rules, nonprofit governance requirements. CMACC may face regulations around conservation materials, hazardous waste (from obsolete media formats), and digital preservation standards. No AI Act or blockchain-specific regulatory exposure. Copyright law applies to exhibition and reproduction of artworks. Performance rights and licensing for time-based media exhibitions.
ip_model: Standard museum IP model. Artists retain copyright. Museum holds exhibition and reproduction rights per loan agreements. CMACC conservation documentation IP depends on institutional policy -- ideally open-access, but may be institutionally held. Photographic and video documentation of exhibitions is museum property. No CC licensing or on-chain IP mechanisms.
opt_in_vs_opt_out: Opt-in for all parties. Artists opt in through exhibition agreements. Audiences opt in through attendance. CMACC clients opt in through conservation service agreements. No opt-out mechanism needed. Standard institutional consent model.
platform_dependency: Minimal platform dependency. Canyon is a physical institution not dependent on digital platforms. CMACC may depend on specific software for conservation work (digital preservation tools, format migration software) but these are replaceable. No blockchain, social media, or cloud platform dependency for core operations. The institution's independence from platform risk is a structural strength.
network_effects: Moderate. Canyon benefits from NYC's institutional network effects (proximity to MoMA, Whitney, galleries, collectors). CMACC could create network effects by becoming a hub for conservation expertise, attracting institutional partnerships. The institution contributes to NYC's network position as a global art capital. Limited digital network effects.
post_crash_trajectory: Not directly affected by NFT/crypto crash. Canyon operates in the traditional contemporary art institutional space, which has its own economic cycles but is not tied to crypto markets. The institution's 2026 opening positions it in a post-crash context where the field is consolidating around serious infrastructure. CMACC's launch during this period of institutional maturation is well-timed. [uncertain]
